Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $A$ be a commutative $R$-algebra with
structure map $\eta_A\colon R\to A$ ([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]).

**The subalgebra generated by finitely many elements.** Let $n\in\mathbb N$ and
$a_1,\ldots,a_n\in A$. Iterating the universal property of a polynomial ring
([[thm-universal-property-of-a-polynomial-ring]]) along the recursion
$R[x_1,\ldots,x_{k+1}]=R[x_1,\ldots,x_k][x_{k+1}]$ of
[[def-multivariate-polynomial-ring-by-iteration]] gives a unique unital ring
homomorphism

$$\operatorname{ev}\colon R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\longrightarrow A$$

that agrees with $\eta_A$ on constants and sends $x_i$ to $a_i$ for each $i$;
at each step of the recursion the one-variable universal property supplies
existence and uniqueness of the extension, and at $n=0$ the map is $\eta_A$
itself. Its image is written $R[a_1,\ldots,a_n]$ and is called the
**$R$-subalgebra of $A$ generated by $a_1,\ldots,a_n$**. It is a subring of $A$
containing $\eta_A(R)$, and it is the smallest such subring containing
$a_1,\ldots,a_n$, since any subring with those properties is closed under the
sums and products that make up a polynomial expression. At $n=0$ it is
$\eta_A(R)$, the image of $R$ in $A$.

**Finite type.** $A$ is **of finite type over $R$**, equivalently a **finitely
generated $R$-algebra**, when $A=R[a_1,\ldots,a_n]$ for some $n\in\mathbb N$ and
some $a_1,\ldots,a_n\in A$. Equivalently, $A$ is isomorphic as an $R$-algebra to
a quotient $R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/\mathfrak a$ for some $n\in\mathbb N$ and some
ideal $\mathfrak a$: the map $\operatorname{ev}$ above is then surjective, and
[[thm-first-isomorphism-theorem-rings]] identifies $A$ with
$R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/\ker\operatorname{ev}$; conversely the composite of the
canonical projection with the inclusion of the indeterminates exhibits any such
quotient as generated by the residues of $x_1,\ldots,x_n$.

**Module-finite.** $A$ is **module-finite over $R$**, equivalently a **finite
$R$-algebra**, when $A$ is finitely generated as an $R$-module
([[def-generated-cyclic-finitely-generated-and-free-modules]]) for the action
$r\cdot a=\eta_A(r)a$.

**Module-finite implies finite type.** If $b_1,\ldots,b_n$ generate $A$ as an
$R$-module then $R[b_1,\ldots,b_n]$, being a subring of $A$ that contains
$\eta_A(R)$ and every $b_i$, contains every $R$-linear combination
$\sum_i\eta_A(r_i)b_i$ and hence all of $A$; so $A=R[b_1,\ldots,b_n]$. The
converse fails, and the companion examples page carries a witness.

Let $R$ be a Noetherian commutative ring and let $A$ be a commutative
$R$-algebra of finite type ([[def-finite-type-and-module-finite-algebras]]).
Then $A$ is a Noetherian ring.

Let $R$ be a ring, let $M$ be a left $R$-module and let $S\subseteq M$. Then the
submodule generated by $S$ ([[def-generated-cyclic-finitely-generated-and-free-modules]])
is the set of finite $R$-linear combinations of elements of $S$:

$$\langle S\rangle_R\;=\;\Big\{\,\sum_{i=1}^{k}r_is_i\;:\;k\in\mathbb N,\ r_1,\ldots,r_k\in R,\ s_1,\ldots,s_k\in S\,\Big\},$$

where the term with $k=0$ is the empty sum $0_M$. In particular
$\langle\varnothing\rangle_R=0$. Commutativity of $R$ is not used, and the
elements $s_1,\ldots,s_k$ are not required to be distinct.

Let $R$ be a ring ([[def-ring]]) with zero $0_R$ and identity $1_R$. A subset
$S \subseteq R$ is a **subring** of $R$ when

- **(T1)** $1_R \in S$;
- **(T2)** $x, y \in S$ implies $x + y \in S$;
- **(T3)** $x \in S$ implies $-x \in S$;
- **(T4)** $x, y \in S$ implies $xy \in S$.

**Why $S$ is then a ring, with the same zero and the same identity.** From (T1)
and (T3), $-1_R \in S$, and from (T2), $0_R = 1_R + (-1_R) \in S$. So $S$
contains $0_R$, is closed under addition and closed under additive inverses,
which are exactly conditions (S1), (S2) and (S3) of [[def-subgroup]] for the
abelian group $(R,+,0_R)$; hence $S$ is a subgroup of $(R,+,0_R)$, and
[[def-subgroup]] states that a subgroup with the restricted operation is itself
a group, **whose identity and whose inverses are those of the ambient group**.
So $(S,+,0_R)$ is an abelian group, commutativity being inherited.

By (T4) multiplication restricts to a binary operation on $S$
([[def-binary-operation]]), and that restriction is associative because it is
associative on $R$. By (T1) the element $1_R$ lies in $S$ and satisfies
$1_R x = x = x 1_R$ there, so it is a two-sided identity for the restricted
multiplication ([[def-identity-element]]); thus $(S,\cdot,1_R)$ is a monoid.
Both distributive laws hold in $S$ because they hold in $R$ and are equations
between elements of $S$.

Therefore $(S, +, \cdot, 0_R, 1_R)$ is a ring, and

$$0_S = 0_R, \qquad 1_S = 1_R, \qquad -_S x = -_R x \quad (x \in S).$$

This last line is not decoration: it is what makes a statement proved in $S$
transportable to $R$ without translation, and it is used when a subfield of an
ordered field is shown to inherit the order and when scalars are restricted
along a subfield inclusion.

([[def-subring]]), with $A$ Noetherian. Suppose

* $C=A[t_1,\ldots,t_r]$ is of finite type over $A$, with $r\in\mathbb N$ and
  $t_1,\ldots,t_r\in C$ ([[def-finite-type-and-module-finite-algebras]]);
* $y_1,\ldots,y_n\in C$ generate $C$ as a $B$-module, with $n\ge1$ and
  $y_1=1_C$.

Choose elements $z_{ij}\in B$ for $1\le i\le r$ and $1\le j\le n$, and
$z_{ijk}\in B$ for $1\le i,j,k\le n$, such that

$$t_i=\sum_{j=1}^{n}z_{ij}y_j,\qquad y_iy_j=\sum_{k=1}^{n}z_{ijk}y_k .$$

Let $A'$ be the $A$-subalgebra of $B$ generated by all the $z_{ij}$ and all the
$z_{ijk}$. Then $A\subseteq A'\subseteq B$, the algebra $A'$ is of finite type
over $A$, and $A'$ is a Noetherian ring.

Such coefficients exist, because the $y_j$ generate $C$ as a $B$-module and
$t_i$ and $y_iy_j$ are elements of $C$. They are chosen, not canonical: only
their existence and their finite number are used, and a different choice gives
a possibly different $A'$ with the same properties.

derivations.claim: The set $M=\sum_{j=1}^{n}A'y_j$ is the $A'$-submodule of $C$ generated by $y_1,\ldots,y_n$, by the finite-sum description of a generated submodule; it is in particular an additive subgroup of $C$ closed under multiplication by elements of $A'$. Since $y_1=1_C$ we have $A'=A'y_1\subseteq M$, and therefore $A\subseteq M$ and $1_C\in M$.

$M$ is closed under multiplication, hence is a subring of $C$. It suffices to multiply two generators with coefficients: for $a,a'\in A'$, $(ay_i)(a'y_j)=aa'(y_iy_j)=aa'\sum_{k=1}^{n}z_{ijk}y_k=\sum_{k=1}^{n}(aa'z_{ijk})y_k$, and each $aa'z_{ijk}$ lies in $A'$ because $A'$ is a subring of $B$ containing every $z_{ijk}$. A product of two elements of $M$ expands by distributivity into a finite sum of such terms, so it lies in $M$; with the additive subgroup property and $1_C\in M$ from step 1.1, $M$ is a subring of $C$.

$M$ contains each $t_i$, since $t_i=\sum_{j=1}^{n}z_{ij}y_j$ and every $z_{ij}$ lies in $A'$. So $M$ is a subring of $C$ containing $A$ and $t_1,\ldots,t_r$. But $C=A[t_1,\ldots,t_r]$ is the smallest such subring, so $C\subseteq M$; and $M\subseteq C$ by construction. Hence $C=M$, and $y_1,\ldots,y_n$ generate $C$ as an $A'$-module, so $C$ is module-finite over $A'$.

Now $A'$ is a Noetherian commutative ring, $A'$ is a subring of $C$, and $C$ is module-finite over $A'$; the intermediate-ring clause applied to $A'\subseteq B\subseteq C$ gives that $B$ is module-finite over $A'$.

Let $M$ be a left $R$-module and $S\subseteq M$. The **submodule generated by
$S$** is

$$\langle S\rangle_R:=\bigcap\{N\le M:S\subseteq N\}.$$

The family is nonempty because $M\le M$, and its intersection is a submodule by
[[lem-submodule-criterion-sums-and-intersections]]. Thus $\langle S\rangle_R$
is the smallest submodule of $M$ containing $S$, just as
[[def-generated-subgroup]] defines a generated subgroup.

The module $M$ is **cyclic** if $M=\langle m\rangle_R$ for some $m\in M$, and
**finitely generated** if $M=\langle S\rangle_R$ for some finite $S$. A subset
$B\subseteq M$ is a **basis** if every element of $M$ has a unique expression
as a finite $R$-linear combination of elements of $B$. A module possessing a
basis is a **free $R$-module**.

Let $R$ be a ring, let $M$ be a left $R$-module and let $S\subseteq M$. Then the
submodule generated by $S$ ([[def-generated-cyclic-finitely-generated-and-free-modules]])
is the set of finite $R$-linear combinations of elements of $S$:

$$\langle S\rangle_R\;=\;\Big\{\,\sum_{i=1}^{k}r_is_i\;:\;k\in\mathbb N,\ r_1,\ldots,r_k\in R,\ s_1,\ldots,s_k\in S\,\Big\},$$

where the term with $k=0$ is the empty sum $0_M$. In particular
$\langle\varnothing\rangle_R=0$. Commutativity of $R$ is not used, and the
elements $s_1,\ldots,s_k$ are not required to be distinct.

derivations.claim: Fix a finite $T\subseteq M$ with $\langle T\rangle_R=M$, available because $M$ is finitely generated, and recall the hypothesis $\langle S\rangle_R=M$.

For each $t\in T$ we have $t\in M=\langle S\rangle_R$, so $t=\sum_{i=1}^{k}r_is_i$ for some $k\in\mathbb N$, some $r_1,\ldots,r_k\in R$ and some $s_1,\ldots,s_k\in S$; write $S_t:=\{s_1,\ldots,s_k\}\subseteq S$, a finite set with $t\in\langle S_t\rangle_R$. One such expression is selected for each of the finitely many elements of $T$, so this is a finite sequence of selections and no choice axiom is used.

Put $S':=\bigcup_{t\in T}S_t$. This is a union of finitely many finite sets, hence finite, and $S'\subseteq S$; moreover $S_t\subseteq S'$ gives $\langle S_t\rangle_R\subseteq\langle S'\rangle_R$, so $t\in\langle S'\rangle_R$ for every $t\in T$, that is $T\subseteq\langle S'\rangle_R$.

$\langle S'\rangle_R$ is a submodule of $M$ containing $T$, so it contains the smallest such submodule, namely $\langle T\rangle_R=M$; and $\langle S'\rangle_R\subseteq M$ always. Hence $\langle S'\rangle_R=M$ with $S'\subseteq S$ finite.

Let $M$ be a left $R$-module. A nonempty subset $S\subseteq M$ is a submodule

$$ru+v\in S\qquad(r\in R, u,v\in S).$$

Consequently, the intersection of every nonempty family of submodules is a
submodule, and, for submodules $A,B\le M$,

$$A+B:=\{a+b:a\in A, b\in B\}$$

is a submodule of $M$.

Let $R$ be a ring. A **left $R$-module** is an abelian group $(M,+,0_M)$ with a

For $a,b\in R[x]$ and $n\in\mathbb N$, define

$$ (a+b)_n:=a_n+b_n,\qquad (ab)_n:=\sum_{i+j=n}a_i b_j. $$

The convolution sum is a finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $R$ ([[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]]). Write $0$ for the zero sequence, $1$ for the sequence with coefficient $1_R$ at index $0$ and zero elsewhere, and $x$ for the sequence with coefficient $1_R$ at index $1$ and zero elsewhere. The coefficient sequence supported at $0$ with value $r$ is denoted again by $r$, and a polynomial $a$ is written formally as $\sum_i a_i x^i$.

The closure of these operations and the commutative-ring axioms are established by [[lem-polynomial-operations-preserve-finite-support]] and [[thm-polynomial-ring-is-a-commutative-ring]].

Let $0\ne f=\sum_i a_i x^i\in R[x]$. Its **degree** is the largest natural number $n$ for which $a_n\ne0$, and its **leading coefficient** is $a_n$:

$$ \deg f:=\max\{i\in\mathbb N:a_i\ne0\},\qquad \operatorname{lc}(f):=a_{\deg f}. $$

The maximum exists because the nonempty support is finite. The polynomial $f$ is **monic** when $\operatorname{lc}(f)=1_R$. The zero polynomial has no degree and no leading coefficient. Accordingly, every degree statement below explicitly separates the zero polynomial rather than assigning it a formal degree.

The empty sum is included and equals $0$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $\mathfrak a$ be an ideal of the polynomial
ring $R[x]$ ([[def-polynomial-ring-over-a-commutative-ring]]), and for
$n\in\mathbb N$ set

$$\mathfrak a_n\;:=\;\{0\}\cup\{\operatorname{lc}(f)\;:\;f\in\mathfrak a,\ f\neq0,\ \deg f=n\}\subseteq R .$$

Then $\mathfrak a_n$ is an ideal of $R$ for every $n\in\mathbb N$, and

$$\mathfrak a_0\subseteq\mathfrak a_1\subseteq\mathfrak a_2\subseteq\cdots .$$

The index runs over $\mathbb N$, so the chain begins at $\mathfrak a_0$, whose
members are $0$ together with the nonzero constant polynomials that lie in
$\mathfrak a$.

Adjoining $0$ is not cosmetic. The zero polynomial has no degree and no leading
coefficient ([[def-polynomial-degree-leading-coefficient-and-monic]]), so it
contributes no element, and without the adjunction the set would be empty
whenever $\mathfrak a$ contains no element of degree exactly $n$.

Let $R$ be a unital ring, $X$ a set, and $M$ a left $R$-module. Every set map $u:X\to M$ extends uniquely to an $R$-module homomorphism $\bar u:R^{(X)}\to M$ satisfying $\bar u(e_x)=u(x)$. Explicitly,
$$\bar u\left(\sum_{x\in F}r_xe_x\right)=\sum_{x\in F}r_xu(x).$$

For a unital ring $R$ and a set $X$, the **free left $R$-module on $X$** is
$$R^{(X)}:=\bigoplus_{x\in X}R.$$
For $x\in X$, the **standard basis vector** $e_x$ has coordinate $1_R$ at $x$ and zero elsewhere. Every element has a unique expression
$$\sum_{x\in F}r_xe_x$$
with $F\subseteq X$ finite. The map $x\mapsto e_x$ is the standard basis inclusion.

More generally, a family $(b_x)_{x\in X}$ is a **basis** of a module $M$ when every element of $M$ is uniquely a finite $R$-linear combination of the $b_x$ ([[def-generated-cyclic-finitely-generated-and-free-modules]]). For $X=\varnothing$, $R^{(X)}=0$ and its empty family is a basis.

Let $R$ be a unital ring and $(M_i)_{i\in I}$ a family of left $R$-modules ([[def-left-and-right-modules]]). Their **direct product** is the module $\prod_{i\in I}M_i$ with coordinatewise operations. The **support** of $m=(m_i)$ is $\{i\in I:m_i\ne0\}$, and the **direct sum** is the submodule
$$\bigoplus_{i\in I}M_i=\{m\in\prod_{i\in I}M_i:\operatorname{supp}(m)\text{ is finite}\}$$
([[def-submodule]]).

This subset is a submodule because the support of a sum is contained in the union of two finite supports and scalar multiplication cannot enlarge support.

For each $i$, the coordinate inclusion $\jmath_i:M_i\to\bigoplus_jM_j$ puts its input in coordinate $i$ and zero elsewhere. If $I=\varnothing$, both product and direct sum are the zero module.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $M,N$ be $R$-modules. Then the abelian
group $\operatorname{Hom}_R(M,N)$ of [[def-hom-groups-and-induced-hom-maps]]
becomes an $R$-module under the pointwise scalar action

$$(rf)(m):=r\,f(m)\qquad(r\in R,\ f\in\operatorname{Hom}_R(M,N),\ m\in M).$$

The underlying additive group is the published one, unchanged: this extends the
abelian-group structure rather than replacing it. Commutativity of $R$ is used,
and is used only to see that $rf$ is again $R$-linear.

It is surjective: given $(y_1,\ldots,y_n)\in N^n$, the set map $i\mapsto y_i$ extends to a homomorphism $f\colon R^n\to N$ with $f(e_i)=y_i$, so $\Phi(f)=(y_1,\ldots,y_n)$.

$\Phi$ is $R$-linear. Addition in $\operatorname{Hom}_R(R^n,N)$ and in $N^n$ is pointwise and coordinatewise respectively, so $\Phi(f+g)=\big((f+g)(e_1),\ldots\big)=\Phi(f)+\Phi(g)$; and the scalar action on the source is pointwise, so $\Phi(rf)=\big(rf(e_1),\ldots,rf(e_n)\big)=r\,\Phi(f)$.

For a homomorphism $u:M\to N$ and any module $X$, **postcomposition** and **precomposition** give homomorphisms
$$u_*:\operatorname{Hom}_R(X,M)\to\operatorname{Hom}_R(X,N),\quad f\mapsto u\circ f,$$
$$u^*:\operatorname{Hom}_R(N,X)\to\operatorname{Hom}_R(M,X),\quad g\mapsto g\circ u.$$
Composition is associative, so $(v\circ u)_*=v_*\circ u_*$ and $(v\circ u)^*=u^*\circ v^*$; identity maps induce identity maps.

A ring $R$ ([[def-ring]]) is **commutative** when its multiplication is
commutative ([[def-binary-operation]]):

$$xy \;=\; yx \qquad \text{for all } x, y \in R .$$

Addition is commutative in every ring, by axiom (R1), so the word refers to
multiplication alone.

Let $R$ be a ring. A **left $R$-module** is an abelian group $(M,+,0_M)$ with a
scalar action $R\times M\to M$, $(r,m)\mapsto rm$, satisfying

$$r(m+n)=rm+rn,\quad (r+s)m=rm+sm,\quad (rs)m=r(sm),\quad 1_Rm=m.$$

A **right $R$-module** has an action $M\times R\to M$, $(m,r)\mapsto mr$, with
the analogous right-handed axioms. Unless “right” is stated, **module** means a
unital left module.

For left $R$-modules $M,N$, a function $f:M\to N$ is an **$R$-module
homomorphism** if

$$f(m+m')=f(m)+f(m')\quad\text{and}\quad f(rm)=rf(m)$$

for all $m,m'\in M$ and $r\in R$. It is a **module isomorphism** if it is a
bijective module homomorphism.

Its **kernel** and **image** are

$$\ker f:=\{m\in M:f(m)=0_N\},\qquad\operatorname{im}f:=\{f(m):m\in M\}.$$

Once [[thm-module-kernel-image-and-injectivity]] establishes that the image is a
submodule, the **cokernel** of $f$ is the quotient module
$\operatorname{coker}f:=N/\operatorname{im}f$.

Ideal criteria and intersections of ideals.

A nonempty subset $I\subseteq R$ is a two-sided ideal exactly when it is closed
under $x-y$ and under $rx,xr$ for all $r\in R$, $x,y\in I$.  Any intersection
of two-sided ideals is a two-sided ideal, with the empty intersection equal to
$R$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $f,g\in R[x]$ be nonzero.

1. If $f+g\ne0$, then $\deg(f+g)\le\max\{\deg f,\deg g\}$.
2. The coefficient of $x^{\deg f+\deg g}$ in $fg$ is $\operatorname{lc}(f)\operatorname{lc}(g)$. If $fg\ne0$, then $\deg(fg)\le\deg f+\deg g$.

Left, right and two-sided ideals.

Let $R$ be a ring. An additive subgroup $I\le(R,+)$ is a **left ideal** when
$r i\in I$ for every $r\in R$ and $i\in I$, and a **right ideal** when
$i r\in I$ for every such $r,i$.  A **two-sided ideal**, written
$I\mathrel{\trianglelefteq}R$, is both a left and a right ideal.  In a
commutative ring these three notions agree.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring. A subset $S\subseteq R$ is **multiplicative** if $1\in S$ and $s,t\in S$ implies $st\in S$.

On $R\times S$, define
$$ (r,s)\sim(r',s')\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad u(rs'-r's)=0\text{ for some }u\in S. $$
The **localisation** of $R$ at $S$, denoted $S^{-1}R$, is the set of equivalence classes for this relation. The class of $(r,s)$ is written $r/s$, and its arithmetic is
$$ \frac r s+\frac{r'}{s'}=\frac{rs'+r's}{ss'},\qquad \frac r s\frac{r'}{s'}=\frac{rr'}{ss'}. $$
The **localisation map** is the ring homomorphism
$$ \lambda_S:R\longrightarrow S^{-1}R,\qquad r\longmapsto r/1. $$
Every $s\in S$ maps to a unit, with $(s/1)^{-1}=1/s$. The construction permits $0\in S$; in that case the localisation is the zero ring.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $S\subseteq R$ multiplicative. For an ideal $I\subseteq R$, write
$$ S^{-1}I=\{r/s:r\in I,\ s\in S\},\qquad I^{\mathrm{sat}}=\{r\in R:sr\in I\text{ for some }s\in S\}. $$
An ideal is **$S$-saturated** when $I=I^{\mathrm{sat}}$. Extension $I\mapsto S^{-1}I$ and contraction $J\mapsto\lambda_S^{-1}(J)$ give inverse inclusion-preserving bijections between $S$-saturated ideals of $R$ and ideals of $S^{-1}R$. Moreover, they restrict to inverse bijections
$$ \{\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Spec}R:\mathfrak p\cap S=\varnothing\}\longleftrightarrow\operatorname{Spec}(S^{-1}R),\qquad \mathfrak p\longmapsto S^{-1}\mathfrak p. $$

In a commutative ring, $(S)$ consists of finite sums $\sum r_i s_i$, and $(a)=Ra$.

The empty sum is included and equals $0$.

The ideal generated by a subset and principal ideals.

For $S\subseteq R$, define $(S)$ to be the intersection of all two-sided ideals
of $R$ containing $S$.  This family is nonempty because it contains $R$, and
[[lem-ideal-criterion-and-intersections]] shows that $(S)$ is an ideal.  For
$a\in R$, the ideal $(\{a\})$ is written $(a)$ and is called **principal**.

citations.quote:
Left, right and two-sided ideals.

Let $R$ be a ring. An additive subgroup $I\le(R,+)$ is a **left ideal** when
$r i\in I$ for every $r\in R$ and $i\in I$, and a **right ideal** when
$i r\in I$ for every such $r,i$.  A **two-sided ideal**, written
$I\mathrel{\trianglelefteq}R$, is both a left and a right ideal.  In a
commutative ring these three notions agree.

The ideal generated by a subset and principal ideals.

For $S\subseteq R$, define $(S)$ to be the intersection of all two-sided ideals
of $R$ containing $S$.  This family is nonempty because it contains $R$, and
[[lem-ideal-criterion-and-intersections]] shows that $(S)$ is an ideal.  For
$a\in R$, the ideal $(\{a\})$ is written $(a)$ and is called **principal**.

In a commutative ring, $(S)$ consists of finite sums $\sum r_i s_i$, and $(a)=Ra$.

The empty sum is included and equals $0$.

Ideal criteria and intersections of ideals.

A nonempty subset $I\subseteq R$ is a two-sided ideal exactly when it is closed
under $x-y$ and under $rx,xr$ for all $r\in R$, $x,y\in I$.  Any intersection
of two-sided ideals is a two-sided ideal, with the empty intersection equal to
$R$.

Let $(P, \le)$ be a poset ([[def-partial-order]]). A subset $C \subseteq P$ is a
**chain** if any two of its elements are comparable: for all $x, y \in C$, either
$x \le y$ or $y \le x$.

Equivalently, $C$ is a chain if the restriction of $\le$ to $C$ is a total order
on $C$.

Let $(P, \le)$ be a poset ([[def-partial-order]]) and $m \in P$.

$m$ is a **maximal element** of $P$ if no element of $P$ is strictly above it:
there is no $x \in P$ with $m < x$. Equivalently, for every $x \in P$, if
$m \le x$ then $x = m$.

$m$ is a **greatest element** (or **maximum**) of $P$ if $x \le m$ for every
$x \in P$.

**Minimal** and **least** elements are defined dually, reversing every
inequality.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $(P, \le)$ be a
nonempty poset in which **every chain has an upper bound**. Then $P$ has a
maximal element ([[def-maximal-element]]).

Note the hypothesis asks only for an upper bound, not a least upper bound, and
the conclusion asserts only that a maximal element exists, never that a greatest
one does.

derivations.claim: Inclusion partially orders $\Sigma$, and $\Sigma$ is nonempty by hypothesis. The empty chain is bounded in $\Sigma$: its upper bounds are all the elements of $\Sigma$, and there is at least one.

Let $\mathcal C\subseteq\Sigma$ be a nonempty chain and put $U:=\bigcup\mathcal C$. Then $U$ is an ideal of $R$. It is nonempty, since some $I\in\mathcal C$ contains $0$. For $x,y\in U$ pick $I,J\in\mathcal C$ with $x\in I$ and $y\in J$; the two are comparable, so both lie in the larger one, whose being an ideal gives $x-y$ there and hence in $U$. For $r\in R$ and $x\in U$, choosing $I\in\mathcal C$ with $x\in I$ gives $rx\in I\subseteq U$. The ideal criterion applies.

$U$ is not finitely generated, so $U\in\Sigma$ and $U$ is an upper bound of $\mathcal C$. Suppose instead $U=(u_1,\ldots,u_k)$ with $k\in\mathbb N$; each $u_i$ lies in $U$, hence in some member of $\mathcal C$. A nonempty finite subset of a chain has a greatest member, by induction on its size using comparability of any two elements, so there is $I\in\mathcal C$ containing every $u_i$; when $k=0$ take any $I\in\mathcal C$, which exists because $\mathcal C$ is nonempty. Then $U=(u_1,\ldots,u_k)\subseteq I\subseteq U$, so $I=U$ is finitely generated, contradicting $I\in\Sigma$.

Every chain in $\Sigma$, empty or not, therefore has an upper bound in $\Sigma$, and $\Sigma$ is nonempty; Zorn's lemma gives a maximal element of $\Sigma$. This is the one place the argument leaves ZF, and it uses the full axiom of choice rather than a countable or dependent form.

Prime ideals and maximal ideals in a commutative ring.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring. A proper ideal $P\subsetneq R$ is **prime** when
$ab\in P$ implies $a\in P$ or $b\in P$. A proper ideal $M\subsetneq R$ is
**maximal** when there is no proper ideal strictly between $M$ and $R$; equivalently,
it is a maximal element of the poset of proper ideals ordered by inclusion.

In a commutative ring, $(S)$ consists of finite sums $\sum r_i s_i$, and $(a)=Ra$.

The empty sum is included and equals $0$.

The ideal generated by a subset and principal ideals.

For $S\subseteq R$, define $(S)$ to be the intersection of all two-sided ideals
of $R$ containing $S$.  This family is nonempty because it contains $R$, and
[[lem-ideal-criterion-and-intersections]] shows that $(S)$ is an ideal.  For
$a\in R$, the ideal $(\{a\})$ is written $(a)$ and is called **principal**.

The sum $I+J$ and product $IJ$ of two-sided ideals.

For two-sided ideals $I,J\mathrel{\trianglelefteq}R$, set

$$I+J:=\{i+j:i\in I,\ j\in J\},\qquad IJ:=\left\{\sum_{k=1}^m i_kj_k:m\ge0,\ i_k\in I,\ j_k\in J\right\}.$$

The empty sum in the definition of $IJ$ is $0$.

Ideal criteria and intersections of ideals.

A nonempty subset $I\subseteq R$ is a two-sided ideal exactly when it is closed
under $x-y$ and under $rx,xr$ for all $r\in R$, $x,y\in I$.  Any intersection
of two-sided ideals is a two-sided ideal, with the empty intersection equal to
$R$.

Every element of $\mathfrak p+(a)$ has the form $x+wa$ with $x\in\mathfrak p$ and $w\in R$, because $(a)=Ra$; so a finite generating list may be written $x_1+w_1a,\ldots,x_n+w_na$ with $x_i\in\mathfrak p$, $w_i\in R$ and $n\in\mathbb N$.

It contains $\mathfrak p$, since $xa\in\mathfrak p$ for $x\in\mathfrak p$, and it contains $b$, since $ba=ab\in\mathfrak p$; as $b\notin\mathfrak p$ the containment $\mathfrak p\subseteq\mathfrak q$ is strict, so by maximality $\mathfrak q$ is finitely generated, say $\mathfrak q=(q_1,\ldots,q_m)$ with $m\in\mathbb N$.

The set $a\mathfrak q$ is an ideal, being closed under differences and under multiplication by $R$ because $\mathfrak q$ is, and it is generated by $aq_1,\ldots,aq_m$: any $q\in\mathfrak q$ is $\sum_jr_jq_j$, so $aq=\sum_jr_j(aq_j)$. Moreover $a\mathfrak q\subseteq\mathfrak p$ by the definition of $\mathfrak q$.

$\mathfrak p=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)+a\mathfrak q$. The inclusion from right to left holds because each $x_i$ lies in $\mathfrak p$ and $a\mathfrak q\subseteq\mathfrak p$. For the other inclusion take $z\in\mathfrak p\subseteq\mathfrak p+(a)$ and write $z=\sum_{i=1}^{n}c_i(x_i+w_ia)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}c_ix_i+ya$ with $c_i\in R$ and $y=\sum_{i=1}^{n}c_iw_i$; then $ya=z-\sum_ic_ix_i$ lies in $\mathfrak p$, so $y\in\mathfrak q$ and $ya\in a\mathfrak q$, whence $z\in(x_1,\ldots,x_n)+a\mathfrak q$.

Both summands are finitely generated, so $\mathfrak p=(x_1,\ldots,x_n,aq_1,\ldots,aq_m)$ is finitely generated, contradicting $\mathfrak p\in\Sigma$. citations.quote:
Let $G$ be a group ([[def-group]]) and $C$ a commutative ring. An **action of
$G$ on $C$ by ring automorphisms** is a left action $G\times C\to C$
([[def-group-action]]), written $(g,c)\mapsto g\cdot c$, such that for every
$g\in G$ the map $c\mapsto g\cdot c$ is a ring homomorphism
([[def-ring-homomorphism]]). Each such map is then automatically bijective,
with inverse the map given by $g^{-1}$, since
$g^{-1}\cdot(g\cdot c)=(g^{-1}g)\cdot c=c$ and likewise in the other order; so
each $g$ acts as a ring automorphism, and in particular $g\cdot1_C=1_C$ and
$g\cdot0_C=0_C$.

The **invariant subring** is

$$C^{G}:=\{\,c\in C\;:\;g\cdot c=c\ \text{ for every }g\in G\,\}.$$

**It is a subring of $C$** ([[def-subring]]). It contains $1_C$, because every
$g$ acts as a unital ring homomorphism; and for $c,c'\in C^{G}$ and $g\in G$ one
has $g\cdot(c+c')=g\cdot c+g\cdot c'=c+c'$, $g\cdot(-c)=-(g\cdot c)=-c$ and
$g\cdot(cc')=(g\cdot c)(g\cdot c')=cc'$, so $C^{G}$ satisfies (T1) to (T4).

**Actions by algebra automorphisms.** When $C$ is a commutative $A$-algebra with
structure map $\eta_C\colon A\to C$ ([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]),
an action **by $A$-algebra automorphisms** is one in which every $g$ fixes
$\eta_C(A)$ pointwise: $g\cdot\eta_C(a)=\eta_C(a)$ for all $g\in G$ and $a\in A$.
Then $\eta_C(A)\subseteq C^{G}$, so $C^{G}$ is an $A$-subalgebra of $C$ and
$A\subseteq C^{G}\subseteq C$ whenever $A$ is a subring of $C$.

**The trivial group.** If $G=\{e\}$ then $e\cdot c=c$ for every $c$, so
$C^{G}=C$.

A **group** is a monoid $(G,*,e)$ ([[def-semigroup-and-monoid]]) in which every
element is invertible ([[def-invertible-element]]). Written out, a group is a set
$G$ with a binary operation $*$ ([[def-binary-operation]]) and an element
$e \in G$ such that

- **(G1)** $(x * y) * z = x * (y * z)$ for all $x, y, z \in G$;
- **(G2)** $e * x = x = x * e$ for every $x \in G$;
- **(G3)** for every $x \in G$ there is $y \in G$ with $y * x = e = x * y$.

By [[lem-identity-unique]] the element $e$ of (G2) is unique, and by
[[lem-inverse-unique]] the element $y$ of (G3) is unique for each $x$ and is
determined by either one of the two equations alone. So the notations $e$ for the
identity and $x^{-1}$ for the inverse of $x$ are legitimate, and asserting
$y * x = e$ alone already says $y = x^{-1}$.

A group is **abelian**, or **commutative**, when its operation is commutative:
$x * y = y * x$ for all $x, y \in G$.

**Notation.** The operation is usually written multiplicatively, $xy$ for
$x * y$, with identity $e$ (or $1$) and inverse $x^{-1}$. For an abelian group it
is often written additively, $x + y$, with identity $0$ and inverse $-x$; the two
notations describe the same notion and nothing below depends on the choice. We
write $G$ for the group when the operation is understood.

**transitive** when every $x,y\in X$ satisfy $g\cdot x=y$ for some $g\in G$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring. The following are equivalent.

1. $R$ is Noetherian ([[def-noetherian-ring]]).
2. Every ideal of $R$ is finitely generated: for every ideal $\mathfrak a$ there
   are finitely many $a_1,\ldots,a_n\in\mathfrak a$, with $n\in\mathbb N$, such
   that $\mathfrak a=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)$.
3. **Ascending chain condition.** Every chain of ideals
   $\mathfrak a_0\subseteq\mathfrak a_1\subseteq\mathfrak a_2\subseteq\cdots$
   indexed by $\mathbb N$ stabilises: there is $N\in\mathbb N$ with
   $\mathfrak a_n=\mathfrak a_N$ for every $n\ge N$.
4. **Maximal condition.** Every nonempty set of ideals of $R$ has a maximal
   member with respect to inclusion.

The implication from the ascending chain condition to the maximal condition uses
dependent choice; the remaining implications are choice-free. The same
attribution is carried by
[[thm-equivalent-characterizations-of-noetherian-modules]], from which this
statement is obtained.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $\mathfrak a$ be an ideal of the polynomial
ring $R[x]$ ([[def-polynomial-ring-over-a-commutative-ring]]), and for
$n\in\mathbb N$ set

$$\mathfrak a_n\;:=\;\{0\}\cup\{\operatorname{lc}(f)\;:\;f\in\mathfrak a,\ f\neq0,\ \deg f=n\}\subseteq R .$$

Then $\mathfrak a_n$ is an ideal of $R$ for every $n\in\mathbb N$, and

$$\mathfrak a_0\subseteq\mathfrak a_1\subseteq\mathfrak a_2\subseteq\cdots .$$

The index runs over $\mathbb N$, so the chain begins at $\mathfrak a_0$, whose
members are $0$ together with the nonzero constant polynomials that lie in
$\mathfrak a$.

Adjoining $0$ is not cosmetic. The zero polynomial has no degree and no leading
coefficient ([[def-polynomial-degree-leading-coefficient-and-monic]]), so it
contributes no element, and without the adjunction the set would be empty
whenever $\mathfrak a$ contains no element of degree exactly $n$.

In a commutative ring, $(S)$ consists of finite sums $\sum r_i s_i$, and $(a)=Ra$.

The empty sum is included and equals $0$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $\mathfrak a$ be an ideal of $R[x]$, let
$n\in\mathbb N$, and let $\mathfrak a_n$ be the stage ideal of
[[lem-leading-coefficient-ideals]]. Suppose $m\in\mathbb N$ and
$g_1,\ldots,g_m\in\mathfrak a$ are nonzero polynomials of degree $n$ whose
leading coefficients $c_j=\operatorname{lc}(g_j)$ generate $\mathfrak a_n$, so
that $\mathfrak a_n=(c_1,\ldots,c_m)$.

Let $f\in\mathfrak a$ be nonzero of degree $d$ with $d\ge n$ and
$\operatorname{lc}(f)\in\mathfrak a_n$. Then there is a polynomial $h$ in the
ideal of $R[x]$ generated by $g_1,\ldots,g_m$ such that

$$f-h=0\qquad\text{or}\qquad f-h\neq0\ \text{ and }\ \deg(f-h)<d .$$

At $d=0$ the second alternative is impossible, so there $f=h$. At $m=0$ the
hypothesis on $f$ cannot be met: $\mathfrak a_n$ is then the zero ideal while a
leading coefficient is nonzero, so the statement is not vacuously producing a
degree drop out of nothing.

Let $0\ne f=\sum_i a_i x^i\in R[x]$. Its **degree** is the largest natural number $n$ for which $a_n\ne0$, and its **leading coefficient** is $a_n$:

$$ \deg f:=\max\{i\in\mathbb N:a_i\ne0\},\qquad \operatorname{lc}(f):=a_{\deg f}. $$

The maximum exists because the nonempty support is finite. The polynomial $f$ is **monic** when $\operatorname{lc}(f)=1_R$. The zero polynomial has no degree and no leading coefficient. Accordingly, every degree statement below explicitly separates the zero polynomial rather than assigning it a formal degree.
Every nonempty subset $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ has a least element: there is $\ell \in S$ with $\ell \le s$ for all $s \in S$.

derivations.claim: The stage ideals form an ascending chain of ideals of $R$ indexed by $\mathbb N$, and $R$ is Noetherian, so that chain stabilises: fix $N\in\mathbb N$ with $\mathfrak a_n=\mathfrak a_N$ for every $n\ge N$.

For each $n\le N$ the ideal $\mathfrak a_n$ of $R$ is finitely generated; discard the zero element from a finite generating set, which changes nothing it generates, and realise each remaining generator $c_{n,j}$ by a nonzero $g_{n,j}\in\mathfrak a$ of degree $n$. This is a selection over the finitely many pairs $(n,j)$ with $n\le N$, so it is a finite selection. Let $\mathfrak b$ be the ideal of $R[x]$ generated by all the $g_{n,j}$; since every $g_{n,j}$ lies in $\mathfrak a$, we have $\mathfrak b\subseteq\mathfrak a$.

Suppose $\mathfrak b\neq\mathfrak a$, so that $\mathfrak a\setminus\mathfrak b$ is nonempty. The zero polynomial lies in $\mathfrak b$, so every element of $\mathfrak a\setminus\mathfrak b$ is nonzero and therefore has a degree; the set of those degrees is a nonempty subset of $\mathbb N$ and so has a least element $d$. Fix $f\in\mathfrak a\setminus\mathfrak b$ with $\deg f=d$.

Put $n=\min(d,N)$, so $n\le N$ and $d\ge n$. If $d\le N$ then $n=d$ and $\operatorname{lc}(f)$ lies in $\mathfrak a_d=\mathfrak a_n$ by the definition of the stage; if $d>N$ then $n=N$ and $\operatorname{lc}(f)\in\mathfrak a_d=\mathfrak a_N=\mathfrak a_n$ by the stabilisation of step 1.1. The polynomials $g_{n,1},\ldots,g_{n,m_n}$ realise generators of $\mathfrak a_n$ at stage $n$, so the cancellation lemma applies and yields $h$ in the ideal generated by them, hence $h\in\mathfrak b$, with $f-h=0$ or $\deg(f-h)<d$.

Both alternatives are impossible. If $f-h=0$ then $f=h\in\mathfrak b$, contradicting $f\in\mathfrak a\setminus\mathfrak b$. If $f-h\ne0$ with $\deg(f-h)<d$, then $f-h$ lies in $\mathfrak a$ and not in $\mathfrak b$, since $h\in\mathfrak b$ and $f\notin\mathfrak b$, so its degree belongs to the set whose least element is $d$, contradicting $\deg(f-h)<d$. Therefore $\mathfrak a=\mathfrak b$, and $\mathfrak a$ is generated by the finitely many $g_{n,j}$.

Let $R$ be a ring ([[def-ring]]) with zero $0_R$ and identity $1_R$. A subset
$S \subseteq R$ is a **subring** of $R$ when

- **(T1)** $1_R \in S$;
- **(T2)** $x, y \in S$ implies $x + y \in S$;
- **(T3)** $x \in S$ implies $-x \in S$;
- **(T4)** $x, y \in S$ implies $xy \in S$.

**Why $S$ is then a ring, with the same zero and the same identity.** From (T1)
and (T3), $-1_R \in S$, and from (T2), $0_R = 1_R + (-1_R) \in S$. So $S$
contains $0_R$, is closed under addition and closed under additive inverses,
which are exactly conditions (S1), (S2) and (S3) of [[def-subgroup]] for the
abelian group $(R,+,0_R)$; hence $S$ is a subgroup of $(R,+,0_R)$, and
[[def-subgroup]] states that a subgroup with the restricted operation is itself
a group, **whose identity and whose inverses are those of the ambient group**.
So $(S,+,0_R)$ is an abelian group, commutativity being inherited.

By (T4) multiplication restricts to a binary operation on $S$
([[def-binary-operation]]), and that restriction is associative because it is
associative on $R$. By (T1) the element $1_R$ lies in $S$ and satisfies
$1_R x = x = x 1_R$ there, so it is a two-sided identity for the restricted
multiplication ([[def-identity-element]]); thus $(S,\cdot,1_R)$ is a monoid.
Both distributive laws hold in $S$ because they hold in $R$ and are equations
between elements of $S$.

Therefore $(S, +, \cdot, 0_R, 1_R)$ is a ring, and

$$0_S = 0_R, \qquad 1_S = 1_R, \qquad -_S x = -_R x \quad (x \in S).$$

This last line is not decoration: it is what makes a statement proved in $S$
transportable to $R$ without translation, and it is used when a subfield of an
ordered field is shown to inherit the order and when scalars are restricted
along a subfield inclusion.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring ([[def-commutative-ring]]). An **$R$-algebra** is a unital ring $A$ together with a unital ring homomorphism

$$\eta_A:R\longrightarrow A$$

([[def-ring-homomorphism]]) whose image is central: $\eta_A(r)a=a\eta_A(r)$ for every $r\in R$ and $a\in A$. The induced scalar action is $ra:=\eta_A(r)a$, making $A$ an $R$-module and multiplication $A\times A\to A$ bilinear.

An **$R$-algebra homomorphism** $f:A\to B$ is a unital ring homomorphism satisfying $f\circ\eta_A=\eta_B$. Such a map is automatically $R$-linear. An $R$-algebra is **commutative** when its underlying ring is commutative.

For left $R$-modules $M,N$, a function $f:M\to N$ is an **$R$-module
homomorphism** if

$$f(m+m')=f(m)+f(m')\quad\text{and}\quad f(rm)=rf(m)$$

for all $m,m'\in M$ and $r\in R$. It is a **module isomorphism** if it is a
bijective module homomorphism.

Its **kernel** and **image** are

$$\ker f:=\{m\in M:f(m)=0_N\},\qquad\operatorname{im}f:=\{f(m):m\in M\}.$$

Once [[thm-module-kernel-image-and-injectivity]] establishes that the image is a
submodule, the **cokernel** of $f$ is the quotient module
$\operatorname{coker}f:=N/\operatorname{im}f$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring. The following are equivalent.

1. $R$ is Noetherian ([[def-noetherian-ring]]).
2. Every ideal of $R$ is finitely generated: for every ideal $\mathfrak a$ there
   are finitely many $a_1,\ldots,a_n\in\mathfrak a$, with $n\in\mathbb N$, such
   that $\mathfrak a=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)$.
3. **Ascending chain condition.** Every chain of ideals
   $\mathfrak a_0\subseteq\mathfrak a_1\subseteq\mathfrak a_2\subseteq\cdots$
   indexed by $\mathbb N$ stabilises: there is $N\in\mathbb N$ with
   $\mathfrak a_n=\mathfrak a_N$ for every $n\ge N$.
4. **Maximal condition.** Every nonempty set of ideals of $R$ has a maximal
   member with respect to inclusion.

The implication from the ascending chain condition to the maximal condition uses
dependent choice; the remaining implications are choice-free. The same
attribution is carried by
[[thm-equivalent-characterizations-of-noetherian-modules]], from which this
statement is obtained.

Let $R$ be a ring, let $M$ be a finitely generated left $R$-module
([[def-generated-cyclic-finitely-generated-and-free-modules]]) and let
$S\subseteq M$ satisfy $\langle S\rangle_R=M$. Then some **finite** subset
$S'\subseteq S$ already satisfies $\langle S'\rangle_R=M$.

No hypothesis is placed on $S$ itself, which may be infinite, and none on $R$
beyond being a ring.

In a commutative ring, $(S)$ consists of finite sums $\sum r_i s_i$, and $(a)=Ra$.

The empty sum is included and equals $0$.

Let $R$ be a ring, let $M$ be a left $R$-module and let $S\subseteq M$. Then the
submodule generated by $S$ ([[def-generated-cyclic-finitely-generated-and-free-modules]])
is the set of finite $R$-linear combinations of elements of $S$:

$$\langle S\rangle_R\;=\;\Big\{\,\sum_{i=1}^{k}r_is_i\;:\;k\in\mathbb N,\ r_1,\ldots,r_k\in R,\ s_1,\ldots,s_k\in S\,\Big\},$$

where the term with $k=0$ is the empty sum $0_M$. In particular
$\langle\varnothing\rangle_R=0$. Commutativity of $R$ is not used, and the
elements $s_1,\ldots,s_k$ are not required to be distinct.

The ideal $\mathfrak aR'$ of $R'$ is exactly the set of finite sums $\sum_i a_ix_i$ with $a_i\in\mathfrak a$ and $x_i\in R'$, which is also the $R'$-submodule of $R'$ generated by the subset $\mathfrak a$; and $\mathfrak aR'$ is finitely generated because $R'$ is Noetherian. Applying the finite-subset lemma to the generating set $\mathfrak a$ of that module produces finitely many elements $a_1,\ldots,a_n\in\mathfrak a$, with $n\in\mathbb N$, generating $\mathfrak aR'$.

Let $a\in\mathfrak a$. By step 2.1 and the description of a generated ideal, $a=\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_ia_i$ for some $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in R'$. Applying $\rho$ and using $\rho(a)=a$ together with $R$-linearity, and noting $a_i\in R$, gives $a=\rho(a)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_i\rho(x_i)$ with every $\rho(x_i)\in R$.

Hence $\mathfrak a\subseteq(a_1,\ldots,a_n)R$, and the reverse inclusion holds because each $a_i$ lies in $\mathfrak a$; so $\mathfrak a=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)R$ is finitely generated. As $\mathfrak a$ was arbitrary, every ideal of $R$ is finitely generated and $R$ is Noetherian.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring ([[def-commutative-ring]]). An **$R$-algebra** is a unital ring $A$ together with a unital ring homomorphism

$$\eta_A:R\longrightarrow A$$

([[def-ring-homomorphism]]) whose image is central: $\eta_A(r)a=a\eta_A(r)$ for every $r\in R$ and $a\in A$. The induced scalar action is $ra:=\eta_A(r)a$, making $A$ an $R$-module and multiplication $A\times A\to A$ bilinear.

An **$R$-algebra homomorphism** $f:A\to B$ is a unital ring homomorphism satisfying $f\circ\eta_A=\eta_B$. Such a map is automatically $R$-linear. An $R$-algebra is **commutative** when its underlying ring is commutative.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $A$ be a commutative $R$-algebra with
structure map $\eta_A\colon R\to A$ ([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]).

**The subalgebra generated by finitely many elements.** Let $n\in\mathbb N$ and
$a_1,\ldots,a_n\in A$. Iterating the universal property of a polynomial ring
([[thm-universal-property-of-a-polynomial-ring]]) along the recursion
$R[x_1,\ldots,x_{k+1}]=R[x_1,\ldots,x_k][x_{k+1}]$ of
[[def-multivariate-polynomial-ring-by-iteration]] gives a unique unital ring
homomorphism

$$\operatorname{ev}\colon R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\longrightarrow A$$

that agrees with $\eta_A$ on constants and sends $x_i$ to $a_i$ for each $i$;
at each step of the recursion the one-variable universal property supplies
existence and uniqueness of the extension, and at $n=0$ the map is $\eta_A$
itself. Its image is written $R[a_1,\ldots,a_n]$ and is called the
**$R$-subalgebra of $A$ generated by $a_1,\ldots,a_n$**. It is a subring of $A$
containing $\eta_A(R)$, and it is the smallest such subring containing
$a_1,\ldots,a_n$, since any subring with those properties is closed under the
sums and products that make up a polynomial expression. At $n=0$ it is
$\eta_A(R)$, the image of $R$ in $A$.

**Finite type.** $A$ is **of finite type over $R$**, equivalently a **finitely
generated $R$-algebra**, when $A=R[a_1,\ldots,a_n]$ for some $n\in\mathbb N$ and
some $a_1,\ldots,a_n\in A$. Equivalently, $A$ is isomorphic as an $R$-algebra to
a quotient $R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/\mathfrak a$ for some $n\in\mathbb N$ and some
ideal $\mathfrak a$: the map $\operatorname{ev}$ above is then surjective, and
[[thm-first-isomorphism-theorem-rings]] identifies $A$ with
$R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/\ker\operatorname{ev}$; conversely the composite of the
canonical projection with the inclusion of the indeterminates exhibits any such
quotient as generated by the residues of $x_1,\ldots,x_n$.

**Module-finite.** $A$ is **module-finite over $R$**, equivalently a **finite
$R$-algebra**, when $A$ is finitely generated as an $R$-module
([[def-generated-cyclic-finitely-generated-and-free-modules]]) for the action
$r\cdot a=\eta_A(r)a$.

**Module-finite implies finite type.** If $b_1,\ldots,b_n$ generate $A$ as an
$R$-module then $R[b_1,\ldots,b_n]$, being a subring of $A$ that contains
$\eta_A(R)$ and every $b_i$, contains every $R$-linear combination
$\sum_i\eta_A(r_i)b_i$ and hence all of $A$; so $A=R[b_1,\ldots,b_n]$. The
converse fails, and the companion examples page carries a witness.

Let $R$ be a ring. A **left $R$-module** is an abelian group $(M,+,0_M)$ with a
scalar action $R\times M\to M$, $(r,m)\mapsto rm$, satisfying

$$r(m+n)=rm+rn,\quad (r+s)m=rm+sm,\quad (rs)m=r(sm),\quad 1_Rm=m.$$

A **right $R$-module** has an action $M\times R\to M$, $(m,r)\mapsto mr$, with
the analogous right-handed axioms. Unless “right” is stated, **module** means a
unital left module.

Let $R$ be a ring, let $M$ be a left $R$-module and let $S\subseteq M$. Then the
submodule generated by $S$ ([[def-generated-cyclic-finitely-generated-and-free-modules]])
is the set of finite $R$-linear combinations of elements of $S$:

$$\langle S\rangle_R\;=\;\Big\{\,\sum_{i=1}^{k}r_is_i\;:\;k\in\mathbb N,\ r_1,\ldots,r_k\in R,\ s_1,\ldots,s_k\in S\,\Big\},$$

where the term with $k=0$ is the empty sum $0_M$. In particular
$\langle\varnothing\rangle_R=0$. Commutativity of $R$ is not used, and the
elements $s_1,\ldots,s_k$ are not required to be distinct.

([[def-subring]]), with $A$ Noetherian. Suppose

* $C=A[t_1,\ldots,t_r]$ is of finite type over $A$, with $r\in\mathbb N$ and

* $y_1,\ldots,y_n\in C$ generate $C$ as a $B$-module, with $n\ge1$ and
  $y_1=1_C$.

Choose elements $z_{ij}\in B$ for $1\le i\le r$ and $1\le j\le n$, and
$z_{ijk}\in B$ for $1\le i,j,k\le n$, such that

$$t_i=\sum_{j=1}^{n}z_{ij}y_j,\qquad y_iy_j=\sum_{k=1}^{n}z_{ijk}y_k .$$

over $A$, and $A'$ is a Noetherian ring.

$t_i$ and $y_iy_j$ are elements of $C$. They are chosen, not canonical: only
their existence and their finite number are used, and a different choice gives
a possibly different $A'$ with the same properties.

commutative rings $A\subseteq B\subseteq C$, each a subring of the next, with

module-finite over $A'$; and $B$ is module-finite over $A'$ as well
([[def-finite-type-and-module-finite-algebras]]).

Let $R$ be a ring ([[def-ring]]) with zero $0_R$ and identity $1_R$. A subset
$S \subseteq R$ is a **subring** of $R$ when

- **(T1)** $1_R \in S$;
- **(T2)** $x, y \in S$ implies $x + y \in S$;
- **(T3)** $x \in S$ implies $-x \in S$;
- **(T4)** $x, y \in S$ implies $xy \in S$.

**Why $S$ is then a ring, with the same zero and the same identity.** From (T1)
and (T3), $-1_R \in S$, and from (T2), $0_R = 1_R + (-1_R) \in S$. So $S$
contains $0_R$, is closed under addition and closed under additive inverses,
which are exactly conditions (S1), (S2) and (S3) of [[def-subgroup]] for the
abelian group $(R,+,0_R)$; hence $S$ is a subgroup of $(R,+,0_R)$, and
[[def-subgroup]] states that a subgroup with the restricted operation is itself
a group, **whose identity and whose inverses are those of the ambient group**.
So $(S,+,0_R)$ is an abelian group, commutativity being inherited.

By (T4) multiplication restricts to a binary operation on $S$
([[def-binary-operation]]), and that restriction is associative because it is
associative on $R$. By (T1) the element $1_R$ lies in $S$ and satisfies
$1_R x = x = x 1_R$ there, so it is a two-sided identity for the restricted
multiplication ([[def-identity-element]]); thus $(S,\cdot,1_R)$ is a monoid.
Both distributive laws hold in $S$ because they hold in $R$ and are equations
between elements of $S$.

$$0_S = 0_R, \qquad 1_S = 1_R, \qquad -_S x = -_R x \quad (x \in S).$$

transportable to $R$ without translation, and it is used when a subfield of an
ordered field is shown to inherit the order and when scalars are restricted
along a subfield inclusion.

citations.quote:
Prime ideals and maximal ideals in a commutative ring.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring. A proper ideal $P\subsetneq R$ is **prime** when
$ab\in P$ implies $a\in P$ or $b\in P$. A proper ideal $M\subsetneq R$ is
**maximal** when there is no proper ideal strictly between $M$ and $R$; equivalently,
it is a maximal element of the poset of proper ideals ordered by inclusion.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and suppose at least one ideal of $R$ is not
finitely generated. Let

$$\Sigma:=\{\,\mathfrak a\trianglelefteq R\;:\;\mathfrak a\ \text{is not finitely generated}\,\}$$

be ordered by inclusion. Then $\Sigma$ has a maximal element
([[def-maximal-element]]): an ideal that is not finitely generated and that no
ideal of $\Sigma$ strictly contains.

**This uses Zorn's lemma, hence the axiom of choice** ([[thm-zorn]]). No
Noetherian hypothesis is available: by
[[thm-noetherian-ring-ideal-characterisations]], $\Sigma$ is nonempty exactly
because $R$ is not Noetherian, so the maximal element cannot come from a maximal condition.
Maximal here means maximal in $\Sigma$, not maximal among the proper ideals of
$R$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $\mathfrak p$ be an ideal of $R$ that is
maximal in the set $\Sigma$ of non-finitely-generated ideals of $R$
([[lem-maximal-non-finitely-generated-ideal]]): that is, $\mathfrak p$ is not
finitely generated, and every ideal of $R$ strictly containing $\mathfrak p$ is
finitely generated. Then $\mathfrak p$ is a prime ideal
([[def-prime-and-maximal-ideals]]).

Let $R$ be a commutative ring. The following are equivalent.

1. $R$ is Noetherian ([[def-noetherian-ring]]).
2. Every ideal of $R$ is finitely generated: for every ideal $\mathfrak a$ there
   are finitely many $a_1,\ldots,a_n\in\mathfrak a$, with $n\in\mathbb N$, such
   that $\mathfrak a=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)$.
3. **Ascending chain condition.** Every chain of ideals
   $\mathfrak a_0\subseteq\mathfrak a_1\subseteq\mathfrak a_2\subseteq\cdots$
   indexed by $\mathbb N$ stabilises: there is $N\in\mathbb N$ with
   $\mathfrak a_n=\mathfrak a_N$ for every $n\ge N$.
4. **Maximal condition.** Every nonempty set of ideals of $R$ has a maximal
   member with respect to inclusion.

The implication from the ascending chain condition to the maximal condition uses
dependent choice; the remaining implications are choice-free. The same
attribution is carried by
[[thm-equivalent-characterizations-of-noetherian-modules]], from which this
statement is obtained.

derivations.claim: Suppose $R$ is not Noetherian. By the ideal-level characterisation, some ideal of $R$ is then not finitely generated, so the set $\Sigma$ of non-finitely-generated ideals of $R$ is nonempty.

Since $\Sigma$ is nonempty, it has a maximal element $\mathfrak p$: an ideal that is not finitely generated and that no non-finitely-generated ideal strictly contains. This is where Zorn's lemma is used; no chain condition on $R$ is available, and none is invoked.
That maximal element is a prime ideal of $R$.

By hypothesis every prime ideal of $R$ is finitely generated, so $\mathfrak p$ is finitely generated, contradicting $\mathfrak p\in\Sigma$. The supposition of step 1.1 fails: every ideal of $R$ is finitely generated, and $R$ is Noetherian.

citations.quote: A left $R$-module $M$ is **Noetherian** when every submodule of $M$ is finitely generated ([[def-generated-cyclic-finitely-generated-and-free-modules]]). This finite-generation definition is the convention; its equivalence with ACC and the maximal condition is proved in [[thm-equivalent-characterizations-of-noetherian-modules]].

Let $M$ be a left $R$-module and $S\subseteq M$. The **submodule generated by
$S$** is

$$\langle S\rangle_R:=\bigcap\{N\le M:S\subseteq N\}.$$

The family is nonempty because $M\le M$, and its intersection is a submodule by
[[lem-submodule-criterion-sums-and-intersections]]. Thus $\langle S\rangle_R$
is the smallest submodule of $M$ containing $S$, just as
[[def-generated-subgroup]] defines a generated subgroup.

The module $M$ is **cyclic** if $M=\langle m\rangle_R$ for some $m\in M$, and
**finitely generated** if $M=\langle S\rangle_R$ for some finite $S$. A subset
$B\subseteq M$ is a **basis** if every element of $M$ has a unique expression
as a finite $R$-linear combination of elements of $B$. A module possessing a
basis is a **free $R$-module**.
Every finitely generated left module over a left Noetherian ring is Noetherian. See [[def-noetherian-ring]].

For a unital ring $R$ and a set $X$, the **free left $R$-module on $X$** is
$$R^{(X)}:=\bigoplus_{x\in X}R.$$
For $x\in X$, the **standard basis vector** $e_x$ has coordinate $1_R$ at $x$ and zero elsewhere. Every element has a unique expression
$$\sum_{x\in F}r_xe_x$$
with $F\subseteq X$ finite. The map $x\mapsto e_x$ is the standard basis inclusion.

More generally, a family $(b_x)_{x\in X}$ is a **basis** of a module $M$ when every element of $M$ is uniquely a finite $R$-linear combination of the $b_x$ ([[def-generated-cyclic-finitely-generated-and-free-modules]]). For $X=\varnothing$, $R^{(X)}=0$ and its empty family is a basis.

Let $R$ be a unital ring, $X$ a set, and $M$ a left $R$-module. Every set map $u:X\to M$ extends uniquely to an $R$-module homomorphism $\bar u:R^{(X)}\to M$ satisfying $\bar u(e_x)=u(x)$. Explicitly,
$$\bar u\left(\sum_{x\in F}r_xe_x\right)=\sum_{x\in F}r_xu(x).$$

Let $R$ be a ring, let $M$ be a left $R$-module and let $S\subseteq M$. Then the
submodule generated by $S$ ([[def-generated-cyclic-finitely-generated-and-free-modules]])
is the set of finite $R$-linear combinations of elements of $S$:

$$\langle S\rangle_R\;=\;\Big\{\,\sum_{i=1}^{k}r_is_i\;:\;k\in\mathbb N,\ r_1,\ldots,r_k\in R,\ s_1,\ldots,s_k\in S\,\Big\},$$

where the term with $k=0$ is the empty sum $0_M$. In particular
$\langle\varnothing\rangle_R=0$. Commutativity of $R$ is not used, and the
elements $s_1,\ldots,s_k$ are not required to be distinct.

A sequence of left $R$-modules and homomorphisms
$$\cdots\longrightarrow M_{i-1}\xrightarrow{d_{i-1}}M_i\xrightarrow{d_i}M_{i+1}\longrightarrow\cdots$$
is **exact at $M_i$** if $\operatorname{im}d_{i-1}=\ker d_i$ ([[def-module-homomorphism-kernel-image-and-cokernel]]). It is **exact** if it is exact at every displayed module at which two arrows meet.

A **short exact sequence** is an exact sequence
$$0\longrightarrow A\xrightarrow{i}B\xrightarrow{p}C\longrightarrow0.$$
Thus $i$ is injective, $p$ is surjective, and $\operatorname{im}i=\ker p$ ([[thm-module-kernel-image-and-injectivity]]).

Let $R$ be a commutative ring. For $n\in\mathbb N$ write $R^n$ for the free
$R$-module $R^{(\{1,\ldots,n\})}$ on an $n$-element set, with standard basis
$e_1,\ldots,e_n$ ([[def-free-module-on-a-set-and-standard-basis]]); at $n=0$ the
index set is empty and $R^0=0$.

**Finitely presented modules.** An $R$-module $M$ is **finitely presented** when
there are $m,n\in\mathbb N$ and module homomorphisms making

$$R^{m}\xrightarrow{\ \alpha\ }R^{n}\xrightarrow{\ \beta\ }M\longrightarrow0$$

an exact sequence ([[def-exact-and-short-exact-sequences-of-modules]]): that is,
$\operatorname{im}\alpha=\ker\beta$ and $\beta$ is surjective
([[def-module-homomorphism-kernel-image-and-cokernel]]).

**The equivalent quotient form.** $M$ is finitely presented exactly when
$M\cong R^{n}/K$ for some $n\in\mathbb N$ and some finitely generated submodule
$K\le R^{n}$ ([[def-generated-cyclic-finitely-generated-and-free-modules]]).
Given a presentation, put $K=\ker\beta=\operatorname{im}\alpha$, which is
generated by $\alpha(e_1),\ldots,\alpha(e_m)$, and
[[thm-first-isomorphism-theorem-modules]] gives $M\cong R^{n}/K$. Conversely,
given $M\cong R^{n}/K$ with $K$ generated by $k_1,\ldots,k_m$, the universal
property of the free module ([[thm-universal-property-of-free-modules]])
supplies $\alpha\colon R^{m}\to R^{n}$ with $\alpha(e_j)=k_j$, whose image is
$K$, and composing the canonical projection with the isomorphism gives $\beta$;
the displayed sequence is then exact.

**Finitely presented algebras.** A commutative $R$-algebra $A$ is **finitely
presented** when there are $n\in\mathbb N$ and a finitely generated ideal
$\mathfrak a\subseteq R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$
([[def-generated-and-principal-ideals]]) with $A\cong R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/\mathfrak a$
as an $R$-algebra.

**Finitely presented implies finitely generated, in both senses.** A finitely
presented module is generated by $\beta(e_1),\ldots,\beta(e_n)$, since $\beta$
is surjective. A finitely presented algebra is of finite type
([[def-finite-type-and-module-finite-algebras]]), being a quotient of
$R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$.

**The boundary values are admitted.** Taking $m=n=0$ presents the zero module,
and taking $m=0$ with $n$ arbitrary presents the free module $R^n$; taking
$\mathfrak a=0$ presents the polynomial algebra itself.

derivations.claim: Condition 1 implies condition 2, because $M$ is a submodule of itself and a Noetherian module has all of its submodules finitely generated.
Condition 2 implies condition 1, since $R$ is a Noetherian ring and a finitely generated module over such a ring is Noetherian.

Condition 3 implies condition 2: an exact sequence $R^m\to R^n\to M\to0$ has its right-hand map $\beta$ surjective, because exactness at $M$ says the image of $\beta$ is the kernel of the zero map $M\to0$, which is all of $M$; every element of $R^n$ is $\sum_{i=1}^{n}r_ie_i$, so every element of $M$ is $\sum_{i=1}^{n}r_i\beta(e_i)$ and $M$ is generated by the finite set $\{\beta(e_1),\ldots,\beta(e_n)\}$.

Assume condition 2 and fix a finite generating set $m_1,\ldots,m_n$ of $M$, with $n\in\mathbb N$. The universal property of the free module gives an $R$-module homomorphism $\beta\colon R^n\to M$ with $\beta(e_i)=m_i$, and its image is the set of all finite sums $\sum_ir_im_i$, which is $\langle m_1,\ldots,m_n\rangle_R=M$; so $\beta$ is surjective.

Still assuming condition 2, the module $R^n$ is generated by the finite set $\{e_1,\ldots,e_n\}$, hence is Noetherian over the Noetherian ring $R$; therefore its submodule $K:=\ker\beta$ is finitely generated, say by $k_1,\ldots,k_m$ with $m\in\mathbb N$.

Still assuming condition 2, the universal property gives $\alpha\colon R^m\to R^n$ with $\alpha(e_j)=k_j$, whose image is $\langle k_1,\ldots,k_m\rangle_R=K=\ker\beta$; together with the surjectivity of $\beta$ this makes $R^m\to R^n\to M\to0$ exact, so $M$ is finitely presented and condition 2 implies condition 3.

Steps 1.1, 1.2, 1.3 and 3.1 close the cycle: condition 1 gives condition 2, condition 2 gives condition 1 and condition 3, and condition 3 gives condition 2. The three conditions are therefore equivalent.

citations.quote: For every commutative ring $R$, the coefficientwise addition and convolution multiplication of [[def-polynomial-ring-over-a-commutative-ring]] make $R[x]$ a commutative ring. The constant-polynomial map $c\colon R\to R[x]$ is an injective unital ring homomorphism ([[def-ring-homomorphism]]).

Let $R$ be a Noetherian commutative ring and let $\mathfrak a$ be an ideal of
$R[x]$. Let $\mathfrak a_0\subseteq\mathfrak a_1\subseteq\cdots$ be the stage
ideals of [[lem-leading-coefficient-ideals]] and let $N\in\mathbb N$ be an index
at which that chain stabilises, so $\mathfrak a_n=\mathfrak a_N$ for every
$n\ge N$. For each $n\le N$ choose finitely many nonzero elements
$c_{n,1},\ldots,c_{n,m_n}$ of $\mathfrak a_n$ generating it, and for each of
them a polynomial $g_{n,j}\in\mathfrak a$, nonzero of degree $n$, with
$\operatorname{lc}(g_{n,j})=c_{n,j}$.

Then the finitely many polynomials $g_{n,j}$, for $n\le N$ and $1\le j\le m_n$,
generate $\mathfrak a$ as an ideal of $R[x]$. In particular every ideal of
$R[x]$ is finitely generated.

The selections are possible: each $\mathfrak a_n$ is an ideal of the Noetherian
ring $R$, hence has a finite generating set, from which the zero element may be
discarded without loss, and every nonzero element of $\mathfrak a_n$ is by
definition the leading coefficient of some nonzero degree-$n$ element of
$\mathfrak a$. Only finitely many selections are made, so no choice axiom is
used.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring. The following are equivalent.

1. $R$ is Noetherian ([[def-noetherian-ring]]).
2. Every ideal of $R$ is finitely generated: for every ideal $\mathfrak a$ there
   are finitely many $a_1,\ldots,a_n\in\mathfrak a$, with $n\in\mathbb N$, such
   that $\mathfrak a=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)$.
3. **Ascending chain condition.** Every chain of ideals
   $\mathfrak a_0\subseteq\mathfrak a_1\subseteq\mathfrak a_2\subseteq\cdots$
   indexed by $\mathbb N$ stabilises: there is $N\in\mathbb N$ with
   $\mathfrak a_n=\mathfrak a_N$ for every $n\ge N$.
4. **Maximal condition.** Every nonempty set of ideals of $R$ has a maximal
   member with respect to inclusion.

The implication from the ascending chain condition to the maximal condition uses
dependent choice; the remaining implications are choice-free. The same
attribution is carried by
[[thm-equivalent-characterizations-of-noetherian-modules]], from which this
statement is obtained.

citations.quote:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $A$ be a commutative $R$-algebra with
structure map $\eta_A\colon R\to A$ ([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]).

**The subalgebra generated by finitely many elements.** Let $n\in\mathbb N$ and
$a_1,\ldots,a_n\in A$. Iterating the universal property of a polynomial ring
([[thm-universal-property-of-a-polynomial-ring]]) along the recursion
$R[x_1,\ldots,x_{k+1}]=R[x_1,\ldots,x_k][x_{k+1}]$ of
[[def-multivariate-polynomial-ring-by-iteration]] gives a unique unital ring
homomorphism

$$\operatorname{ev}\colon R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\longrightarrow A$$

that agrees with $\eta_A$ on constants and sends $x_i$ to $a_i$ for each $i$;
at each step of the recursion the one-variable universal property supplies
existence and uniqueness of the extension, and at $n=0$ the map is $\eta_A$
itself. Its image is written $R[a_1,\ldots,a_n]$ and is called the
**$R$-subalgebra of $A$ generated by $a_1,\ldots,a_n$**. It is a subring of $A$
containing $\eta_A(R)$, and it is the smallest such subring containing
$a_1,\ldots,a_n$, since any subring with those properties is closed under the
sums and products that make up a polynomial expression. At $n=0$ it is
$\eta_A(R)$, the image of $R$ in $A$.

**Finite type.** $A$ is **of finite type over $R$**, equivalently a **finitely
generated $R$-algebra**, when $A=R[a_1,\ldots,a_n]$ for some $n\in\mathbb N$ and
some $a_1,\ldots,a_n\in A$. Equivalently, $A$ is isomorphic as an $R$-algebra to
a quotient $R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/\mathfrak a$ for some $n\in\mathbb N$ and some
ideal $\mathfrak a$: the map $\operatorname{ev}$ above is then surjective, and
[[thm-first-isomorphism-theorem-rings]] identifies $A$ with
$R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/\ker\operatorname{ev}$; conversely the composite of the
canonical projection with the inclusion of the indeterminates exhibits any such
quotient as generated by the residues of $x_1,\ldots,x_n$.

**Module-finite.** $A$ is **module-finite over $R$**, equivalently a **finite
$R$-algebra**, when $A$ is finitely generated as an $R$-module
([[def-generated-cyclic-finitely-generated-and-free-modules]]) for the action
$r\cdot a=\eta_A(r)a$.

**Module-finite implies finite type.** If $b_1,\ldots,b_n$ generate $A$ as an
$R$-module then $R[b_1,\ldots,b_n]$, being a subring of $A$ that contains
$\eta_A(R)$ and every $b_i$, contains every $R$-linear combination
$\sum_i\eta_A(r_i)b_i$ and hence all of $A$; so $A=R[b_1,\ldots,b_n]$. The
converse fails, and the companion examples page carries a witness.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring ([[def-commutative-ring]]). An **$R$-algebra** is a unital ring $A$ together with a unital ring homomorphism

$$\eta_A:R\longrightarrow A$$

([[def-ring-homomorphism]]) whose image is central: $\eta_A(r)a=a\eta_A(r)$ for every $r\in R$ and $a\in A$. The induced scalar action is $ra:=\eta_A(r)a$, making $A$ an $R$-module and multiplication $A\times A\to A$ bilinear.

An **$R$-algebra homomorphism** $f:A\to B$ is a unital ring homomorphism satisfying $f\circ\eta_A=\eta_B$. Such a map is automatically $R$-linear. An $R$-algebra is **commutative** when its underlying ring is commutative.
Every finitely generated left module over a left Noetherian ring is Noetherian. See [[def-noetherian-ring]].

In a commutative ring, $(S)$ consists of finite sums $\sum r_i s_i$, and $(a)=Ra$.

The empty sum is included and equals $0$.

A left $R$-module $M$ is **Noetherian** when every submodule of $M$ is finitely generated ([[def-generated-cyclic-finitely-generated-and-free-modules]]). This finite-generation definition is the convention; its equivalence with ACC and the maximal condition is proved in [[thm-equivalent-characterizations-of-noetherian-modules]].

Let $R$ be a commutative ring. The following are equivalent.

1. $R$ is Noetherian ([[def-noetherian-ring]]).
2. Every ideal of $R$ is finitely generated: for every ideal $\mathfrak a$ there
   are finitely many $a_1,\ldots,a_n\in\mathfrak a$, with $n\in\mathbb N$, such
   that $\mathfrak a=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)$.
3. **Ascending chain condition.** Every chain of ideals
   $\mathfrak a_0\subseteq\mathfrak a_1\subseteq\mathfrak a_2\subseteq\cdots$
   indexed by $\mathbb N$ stabilises: there is $N\in\mathbb N$ with
   $\mathfrak a_n=\mathfrak a_N$ for every $n\ge N$.
4. **Maximal condition.** Every nonempty set of ideals of $R$ has a maximal
   member with respect to inclusion.

The implication from the ascending chain condition to the maximal condition uses
dependent choice; the remaining implications are choice-free. The same
attribution is carried by
[[thm-equivalent-characterizations-of-noetherian-modules]], from which this
statement is obtained.

Let $M$ be a left $R$-module. A subset $N\subseteq M$ is a **submodule** when
it is a subgroup of the additive group of $M$ and is closed under scalars:

$$r\in R,\ n\in N\quad\Longrightarrow\quad rn\in N.$$

The operations on $N$ are the restrictions of those of $M$. Write $N\le M$ when
the ring and module are understood.

Let $\varphi\colon A\to B$ be a homomorphism of commutative rings, so that $B$ is
an $A$-algebra ([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]) and every $B$-module
becomes an $A$-module through $a\cdot z:=\varphi(a)z$. Suppose $B$ is generated
as an $A$-module by $b_1,\ldots,b_m$ with $m\in\mathbb N$, and let $M$ be a
$B$-module generated as a $B$-module by $u_1,\ldots,u_n$ with $n\in\mathbb N$.
Then the $mn$ products $b_iu_j$ generate $M$ as an $A$-module.

In particular, if $\psi\colon B\to C$ is a homomorphism of commutative rings
making $C$ module-finite over $B$, and $B$ is module-finite over $A$, then $C$
is module-finite over $A$ ([[def-finite-type-and-module-finite-algebras]]): the
products $\psi(b_i)c_j$ of a finite $A$-generating list of $B$ with a finite
$B$-generating list of $C$ generate $C$ over $A$.

derivations.claim: Let $B'$ be any commutative $A$-algebra that is module-finite over $A$. Then $B'$ is a finitely generated module over the Noetherian ring $A$, hence a Noetherian $A$-module: every $A$-submodule of $B'$ is finitely generated over $A$. This applies in particular to $B'=B$.

First clause. Let $\mathfrak b$ be an ideal of $B'$. It is an additive subgroup of $B'$ closed under the $A$-action, since $a\cdot x=\eta_{B'}(a)x\in\mathfrak b$ for $x\in\mathfrak b$, so it is an $A$-submodule and therefore generated over $A$ by finitely many $x_1,\ldots,x_k\in\mathfrak b$. Every element of $\mathfrak b$ is then $\sum_i\eta_{B'}(a_i)x_i$, which lies in the ideal $(x_1,\ldots,x_k)$ of $B'$; and that ideal is contained in $\mathfrak b$ because each $x_i$ lies in $\mathfrak b$. So $\mathfrak b=(x_1,\ldots,x_k)$ is finitely generated as an ideal, and $B'$ is a Noetherian ring. Taking $B'=B$ gives the first clause.

Second clause, first half. Suppose the $A$-algebra structure map is the inclusion $A\subseteq B$ and $C$ is a subring of $B$ with $A\subseteq C\subseteq B$. Then $C$ is an additive subgroup of $B$ closed under the $A$-action, because $a\cdot x=ax$ is a product of two elements of $C$; so $C$ is an $A$-submodule of the Noetherian $A$-module $B$ and is therefore finitely generated as an $A$-module, that is, module-finite over $A$.

Third clause. Let $M$ be a finitely generated $B$-module, say generated over $B$ by $u_1,\ldots,u_n$, and let $b_1,\ldots,b_m$ generate $B$ over $A$. The $mn$ products $b_iu_j$ generate $M$ as an $A$-module, so $M$ is a finitely generated $A$-module and hence a Noetherian $A$-module.

Step 2.2 makes $C$ a commutative $A$-algebra, through the inclusion $A\subseteq C$, that is module-finite over $A$; steps 1.1 and 2.1 were proved for an arbitrary such algebra, so applying them with $B'=C$ makes $C$ a Noetherian ring. With steps 2.1 and 2.3 this establishes all three clauses.

Let $G$ be a group ([[def-group]]) and $C$ a commutative ring. An **action of
$G$ on $C$ by ring automorphisms** is a left action $G\times C\to C$
([[def-group-action]]), written $(g,c)\mapsto g\cdot c$, such that for every
$g\in G$ the map $c\mapsto g\cdot c$ is a ring homomorphism
([[def-ring-homomorphism]]). Each such map is then automatically bijective,
with inverse the map given by $g^{-1}$, since
$g^{-1}\cdot(g\cdot c)=(g^{-1}g)\cdot c=c$ and likewise in the other order; so
each $g$ acts as a ring automorphism, and in particular $g\cdot1_C=1_C$ and
$g\cdot0_C=0_C$.

The **invariant subring** is

$$C^{G}:=\{\,c\in C\;:\;g\cdot c=c\ \text{ for every }g\in G\,\}.$$

**It is a subring of $C$** ([[def-subring]]). It contains $1_C$, because every
$g$ acts as a unital ring homomorphism; and for $c,c'\in C^{G}$ and $g\in G$ one
has $g\cdot(c+c')=g\cdot c+g\cdot c'=c+c'$, $g\cdot(-c)=-(g\cdot c)=-c$ and
$g\cdot(cc')=(g\cdot c)(g\cdot c')=cc'$, so $C^{G}$ satisfies (T1) to (T4).

**Actions by algebra automorphisms.** When $C$ is a commutative $A$-algebra with
structure map $\eta_C\colon A\to C$ ([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]),
an action **by $A$-algebra automorphisms** is one in which every $g$ fixes
$\eta_C(A)$ pointwise: $g\cdot\eta_C(a)=\eta_C(a)$ for all $g\in G$ and $a\in A$.
Then $\eta_C(A)\subseteq C^{G}$, so $C^{G}$ is an $A$-subalgebra of $C$ and
$A\subseteq C^{G}\subseteq C$ whenever $A$ is a subring of $C$.

**The trivial group.** If $G=\{e\}$ then $e\cdot c=c$ for every $c$, so
$C^{G}=C$.

Let $G$ be a **finite** group acting by ring automorphisms on a **nonzero**
commutative ring $C$, and let $C^{G}$ be the invariant subring
([[def-invariant-subring-of-a-group-of-ring-automorphisms]]). Extend the action
to the polynomial ring $C[T]$ coefficientwise, fixing $T$. For $x\in C$ put

$$P_x(T)\;:=\;\prod_{g\in G}\big(T-g\cdot x\big)\in C[T].$$

Then $P_x$ is monic of degree $|G|$, every coefficient of $P_x$ lies in $C^{G}$,
and $P_x(x)=0$. Consequently every element of $C$ is integral over $C^{G}$
([[def-integral-element-and-algebraic-integer]]).

Finiteness of $G$ is a hypothesis, not a convenience: the product is over the
index set $G$ and is a polynomial only because that set is finite. The
hypothesis $C\neq0$ is what makes $1_C\neq0_C$, so that a monic polynomial
exists at all.

Let $A\subseteq B\subseteq C$ be commutative rings, each a subring of the next
([[def-subring]]), with $A$ Noetherian. Suppose $C$ is of finite type over $A$
([[def-finite-type-and-module-finite-algebras]]) and every element of $C$ is
integral over $B$ ([[def-integral-element-and-algebraic-integer]]). Then $C$ is
module-finite over $B$, and $B$ is of finite type over $A$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $A$ be a commutative $R$-algebra with
structure map $\eta_A\colon R\to A$ ([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]).

**The subalgebra generated by finitely many elements.** Let $n\in\mathbb N$ and
$a_1,\ldots,a_n\in A$. Iterating the universal property of a polynomial ring
([[thm-universal-property-of-a-polynomial-ring]]) along the recursion
$R[x_1,\ldots,x_{k+1}]=R[x_1,\ldots,x_k][x_{k+1}]$ of
[[def-multivariate-polynomial-ring-by-iteration]] gives a unique unital ring
homomorphism

$$\operatorname{ev}\colon R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\longrightarrow A$$

that agrees with $\eta_A$ on constants and sends $x_i$ to $a_i$ for each $i$;
at each step of the recursion the one-variable universal property supplies
existence and uniqueness of the extension, and at $n=0$ the map is $\eta_A$
itself. Its image is written $R[a_1,\ldots,a_n]$ and is called the
**$R$-subalgebra of $A$ generated by $a_1,\ldots,a_n$**. It is a subring of $A$
containing $\eta_A(R)$, and it is the smallest such subring containing
$a_1,\ldots,a_n$, since any subring with those properties is closed under the
sums and products that make up a polynomial expression. At $n=0$ it is
$\eta_A(R)$, the image of $R$ in $A$.

**Finite type.** $A$ is **of finite type over $R$**, equivalently a **finitely
generated $R$-algebra**, when $A=R[a_1,\ldots,a_n]$ for some $n\in\mathbb N$ and
some $a_1,\ldots,a_n\in A$. Equivalently, $A$ is isomorphic as an $R$-algebra to
a quotient $R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/\mathfrak a$ for some $n\in\mathbb N$ and some
ideal $\mathfrak a$: the map $\operatorname{ev}$ above is then surjective, and
[[thm-first-isomorphism-theorem-rings]] identifies $A$ with
$R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/\ker\operatorname{ev}$; conversely the composite of the
canonical projection with the inclusion of the indeterminates exhibits any such
quotient as generated by the residues of $x_1,\ldots,x_n$.

**Module-finite.** $A$ is **module-finite over $R$**, equivalently a **finite
$R$-algebra**, when $A$ is finitely generated as an $R$-module
([[def-generated-cyclic-finitely-generated-and-free-modules]]) for the action
$r\cdot a=\eta_A(r)a$.

**Module-finite implies finite type.** If $b_1,\ldots,b_n$ generate $A$ as an
$R$-module then $R[b_1,\ldots,b_n]$, being a subring of $A$ that contains
$\eta_A(R)$ and every $b_i$, contains every $R$-linear combination
$\sum_i\eta_A(r_i)b_i$ and hence all of $A$; so $A=R[b_1,\ldots,b_n]$. The
converse fails, and the companion examples page carries a witness.

Let $R$ be a ring ([[def-ring]]) with zero $0_R$ and identity $1_R$. A subset
$S \subseteq R$ is a **subring** of $R$ when

- **(T1)** $1_R \in S$;
- **(T2)** $x, y \in S$ implies $x + y \in S$;
- **(T3)** $x \in S$ implies $-x \in S$;
- **(T4)** $x, y \in S$ implies $xy \in S$.

**Why $S$ is then a ring, with the same zero and the same identity.** From (T1)
and (T3), $-1_R \in S$, and from (T2), $0_R = 1_R + (-1_R) \in S$. So $S$
contains $0_R$, is closed under addition and closed under additive inverses,
which are exactly conditions (S1), (S2) and (S3) of [[def-subgroup]] for the
abelian group $(R,+,0_R)$; hence $S$ is a subgroup of $(R,+,0_R)$, and
[[def-subgroup]] states that a subgroup with the restricted operation is itself
a group, **whose identity and whose inverses are those of the ambient group**.
So $(S,+,0_R)$ is an abelian group, commutativity being inherited.

By (T4) multiplication restricts to a binary operation on $S$
([[def-binary-operation]]), and that restriction is associative because it is
associative on $R$. By (T1) the element $1_R$ lies in $S$ and satisfies
$1_R x = x = x 1_R$ there, so it is a two-sided identity for the restricted
multiplication ([[def-identity-element]]); thus $(S,\cdot,1_R)$ is a monoid.
Both distributive laws hold in $S$ because they hold in $R$ and are equations
between elements of $S$.

Therefore $(S, +, \cdot, 0_R, 1_R)$ is a ring, and

$$0_S = 0_R, \qquad 1_S = 1_R, \qquad -_S x = -_R x \quad (x \in S).$$

This last line is not decoration: it is what makes a statement proved in $S$
transportable to $R$ without translation, and it is used when a subfield of an
ordered field is shown to inherit the order and when scalars are restricted
along a subfield inclusion.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring. The following are equivalent.

1. $R$ is Noetherian ([[def-noetherian-ring]]).
2. Every ideal of $R$ is finitely generated: for every ideal $\mathfrak a$ there
   are finitely many $a_1,\ldots,a_n\in\mathfrak a$, with $n\in\mathbb N$, such
   that $\mathfrak a=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)$.
3. **Ascending chain condition.** Every chain of ideals
   $\mathfrak a_0\subseteq\mathfrak a_1\subseteq\mathfrak a_2\subseteq\cdots$
   indexed by $\mathbb N$ stabilises: there is $N\in\mathbb N$ with
   $\mathfrak a_n=\mathfrak a_N$ for every $n\ge N$.
4. **Maximal condition.** Every nonempty set of ideals of $R$ has a maximal
   member with respect to inclusion.

The implication from the ascending chain condition to the maximal condition uses
dependent choice; the remaining implications are choice-free. The same
attribution is carried by
[[thm-equivalent-characterizations-of-noetherian-modules]], from which this
statement is obtained.

derivations.claim: Suppose the conclusion fails, and let $\Sigma$ be the set of ideals of $R$ that do not belong to $\mathcal P$; the supposition says exactly that $\Sigma\neq\varnothing$.
Since $R$ is Noetherian and $\Sigma$ is a nonempty set of ideals, it has a maximal member: fix an ideal $I\in\Sigma$ such that no member of $\Sigma$ strictly contains $I$.

Let $J$ be any ideal of $R$ with $I\subsetneq J$. Then $J\notin\Sigma$, for otherwise $J$ would be a member of $\Sigma$ strictly containing $I$, against the maximality fixed in the previous step. So $J\in\mathcal P$, and this holds for every ideal strictly containing $I$.
The hereditary property, applied to the ideal $I$, therefore gives $I\in\mathcal P$. But $I\in\Sigma$ means $I\notin\mathcal P$.

The supposition of step 1.1 is untenable, so $\Sigma=\varnothing$ and $\mathcal P$ contains every ideal of $R$. The only non-constructive input is the maximal element produced in step 2.1, whose dependent-choice cost is the one recorded by the cited characterisation; nothing else in the argument selects anything.
